API 570 Piping Inspector: Exam & Requirements [2026]

Comprehensive guide to API 570 Piping Inspector. Explore principles, standards, and best practices for effective implementation.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · March 2026 · Certification & Career

API 570 Piping Inspector Exam & Requirements: Complete Guide 2026

The API 570 certification is one of the most valuable NDT inspector credentials in the world, opening doors to high-paying positions in oil refining, petrochemicals, and power generation. This guide covers everything you need to know about the API 570 exam and requirements.

API 570 Exam Overview

Eligibility Requirements

Before you can even sit for the API 570 exam, you must meet these prerequisites:

  • ASNT Level III Certification: Must hold current ASNT Level III in minimum 2 NDT methods (Ultrasonic Testing and Penetrant Testing are typical combination)
  • NDT Field Experience: Minimum 5 years of documented non-destructive testing field experience
  • Piping Inspection Experience: Minimum 3 years specific in-service piping inspection experience
  • Education: High school diploma or GED minimum
  • Active Employment: Many companies require current employment in NDT field at time of examination

Typical Path to API 570: 7-8 years total (ASNT Level II → gain experience → ASNT Level III → 3 more years piping specific → eligible for API 570)

Exam Format

Component Details
Total Questions 200 multiple-choice questions
Time Allowed 4 hours (240 minutes)
Passing Score 75% (150 correct answers minimum)
Question Types Recall (20%), Applied Knowledge/Calculations (40%), Scenario-Based (40%)
Exam Cost $500-$800 depending on location
Retake Policy Can retake after 30 days; unlimited attempts allowed

Content Distribution

Content Area % of Exam Question Count
API 570 Code Requirements & Inspection Procedures 30% ~60 questions
Piping Systems Fundamentals & Pressure-Temperature Ratings 20% ~40 questions
NDE Methods & Equipment for Piping 20% ~40 questions
Defect Evaluation & Fitness-for-Service (API 579) 18% ~36 questions
Repair & Alteration Procedures 12% ~24 questions

Core Content Requirements

API 570 Code Knowledge (30% of Exam)

Key Topics:

  • Inspection Authority Responsibilities: Documentation, sign-off authority, procedure approval
  • Inspection Types: VEI (Visual External Inspection), TMI (Thickness Measurement), InSI (Internal Inspection), DE (Direct Examination). Know frequency requirements for each.
  • Risk-Based Inspection (RBI): Categories 1-3, probability of failure vs consequence of failure calculation
  • Inspection Frequencies: VEI minimum annually. TMI based on corrosion rate and RBI category. InSI every 5-15 years depending on risk.
  • Documentation Requirements: Inspection history file, thickness trending, RBI assessments, repair records. Retention: 10 years minimum.
  • Corrosion Rate Calculation: (Original - Current) / Years = mils/year. Affects future inspection planning.
  • Pressure Testing Frequency: After major repairs; every 5-10 years for high-risk systems per RBI.

High-Probability Exam Questions:

  • "A piping section shows thickness drop from 0.312" to 0.218" over 5 years. Calculate corrosion rate in mils/year." (Answer: 18.8 mils/year — high corrosion, requires action)
  • "What is the minimum interval for external visual inspection of in-service piping?" (Answer: 12 months/annually)
  • "Describe the three RBI categories and typical inspection intervals." (Answer: Category 1 every 2-3 years, Category 2 every 5-7 years, Category 3 every 7-10 years)

Piping Systems Fundamentals (20% of Exam)

Pressure-Temperature Ratings:

  • Design pressure: Maximum safe operating pressure; stamped on nameplate
  • Design temperature: Maximum operating temperature
  • Rating charts: Know how pressure rating decreases with increasing temperature
  • Safety factor: Typically 3.5-4.0 on ultimate tensile strength

Piping Materials:

  • Carbon steel (most common) — excellent toughness, prone to corrosion
  • Low-alloy steels (ASTM A335 Gr. P11, P22) — high temperature applications
  • Austenitic stainless steel — corrosion resistant but susceptible to stress corrosion cracking (SCC)
  • Duplex/Super-duplex — increasingly common; intermediate properties
  • Non-ferrous (copper, nickel alloys) — specialty services

Piping Components Knowledge:

  • Elbows: Most erosion-prone; measure wall thickness at multiple angles (top, side, bottom)
  • Tees: Flow separation points; higher corrosion risk; critical inspection areas
  • Reducers: Turbulent flow zone; erosion-corrosion common
  • Flanges: Leak potential; inspect bolt tension and gasket condition
  • Valves: Inspect packing glands, seat wear, flange leakage

NDE Methods for Piping (20% of Exam)

Ultrasonic Thickness (UT): Primary method for piping inspection

  • Accuracy: ±0.01 inch typical
  • Calibration: Mandatory before each shift; zero block + thickness reference block
  • Measurement points: 4-12 per piping section depending on size; 12, 3, 6, 9 o'clock positions
  • Surface conditions: Clean to bare metal; remove paint/scale that affects readings

Magnetic Particle (MPI): For weld inspection on carbon/low-alloy steels

  • Detects: Surface and near-surface cracks/defects in ferromagnetic materials
  • Penetration: 3-5 mm maximum depth
  • NOT suitable for: Austenitic stainless steel (use PT instead)
  • Cost: $2,000-$8,000 per system depending on extent

Liquid Penetrant (PT): For weld inspection on stainless and all materials

  • Detects: Surface-breaking defects/cracks
  • Excellent for: Austenitic stainless steel welds, stress corrosion crack (SCC) detection
  • Sensitivity: 0.1-0.5 mm surface defects
  • Cleaning required: Post-inspection chemical cleaning needed

Eddy Current (ECT): Emerging for piping inspection

  • Best for: Tube/small diameter pipe inspection (tubing runs in heat exchangers)
  • Advantage: Detects subsurface SCC that UT might miss
  • Limitation: Limited by probe design; size/geometry dependent

Defect Evaluation & Fitness-for-Service (18% of Exam)

Corrosion Acceptability:

  • Loss <2% of design thickness: Continue in service; normal inspection
  • Loss 2-10%: Continue; increase inspection frequency
  • Loss 10-25%: Pressure test required; consider repair schedule
  • Loss >25%: Repair immediately or reduce operating pressure

Flaw Sizing (Cracks):

  • Measure length and depth of any crack found
  • Critical flaw length: If length/thickness ratio (a/t) >0.3, likely unacceptable
  • Most cracks >50 mm length require repair
  • Use API 579 to perform fitness-for-service assessment

API 579 FFS Levels:

  • Level 1 (Conservative): Quick assessment; if fails, move to Level 2
  • Level 2 (Detailed): More accurate analysis considering actual geometry/material
  • Level 3 (Advanced): Fracture mechanics; FEA analysis; requires expert

Repair & Alteration (12% of Exam)

Repair Procedure Requirements:

  • Written procedure with calculations per ASME B31.3
  • Design drawings showing repair configuration
  • Material certification and welding parameters
  • Post-repair NDE: 100% visual + MT/PT of weld and HAZ
  • Pressure testing: Typically required for major repairs (test at 1.5× design pressure)

Major vs. Minor Repairs:

  • Minor: Small patch <2" diameter; basic documentation; visual + MPI/PT only
  • Major: Section replacement, affects pressure rating; full engineering package and NDE

Study Strategy (6-Week Prep Plan)

Week 1: API 570 Fundamentals (35 hours)

  • Days 1-2: Read API 570 standard cover to cover (8-10 hours)
  • Days 3-4: Study inspection procedures, frequencies, RBI concepts (10 hours)
  • Days 5-7: Work practice problems on corrosion rate, remaining life (15 hours)
  • Target: Comfortable with inspection terminology and RBI calculation

Week 2: Piping Systems & Materials (30 hours)

  • Days 1-2: Pressure-temperature rating, piping design fundamentals (8 hours)
  • Days 3-5: Material types, corrosion mechanisms in each service (12 hours)
  • Days 6-7: Practice piping-specific scenario questions (10 hours)
  • Target: Know piping materials, pressure ratings, and corrosion drivers

Week 3: NDE Methods in Piping Context (30 hours)

  • Days 1-2: UT for piping measurement (8 hours)
  • Days 3-4: MPI/PT weld inspection (8 hours)
  • Days 5-7: Practice questions on NDE selection and application (14 hours)
  • Target: Know which NDE for which piping material; measurement strategies

Week 4: Fitness-for-Service & Defect Evaluation (30 hours)

  • Days 1-2: API 579 FFS methodology (10 hours)
  • Days 3-5: Corrosion acceptability criteria; pit/crack evaluation (12 hours)
  • Days 6-7: Practice FFS scenario questions (8 hours)
  • Target: Determine acceptability of defects; when repair vs. continue

Week 5: Repair Procedures & Integration (25 hours)

  • Days 1-2: Repair documentation, welding requirements, pressure testing (8 hours)
  • Days 3-7: Take 4 full-length practice exams (4 hours each = 16 hours); review weak areas (1 hour)
  • Target: Identify and strengthen weak knowledge areas before exam week

Week 6: Final Review & Exam Prep (20 hours)

  • Days 1-4: Focused review on weakest topics from practice exams (15 hours)
  • Days 5-6: Light review, mental preparation, rest (5 hours)
  • Day 7: Exam day
  • Target: Build confidence; practice time management under exam conditions

Time Management for Exam Day

Strategy: 240 minutes for 200 questions = 1.2 minutes/question average

  • First Pass (90 min): Answer all questions you're confident about. Flag difficult ones.
  • Second Pass (80 min): Work through harder questions systematically
  • Final Pass (70 min): Review answers; attempt remaining flagged questions; check arithmetic

Tips:

  • Don't spend >3 minutes on any single question
  • For calculations: Show work, double-check units, verify answer reasonableness
  • For scenario questions: Identify the key constraint then apply API 570/579 rule
  • Avoid common pitfalls: Confusing design vs. operating pressure; forgetting corrosion allowance; applying wrong inspection interval

Study Materials & Costs

Essential (Must-Have):

  • API 570 Standard (latest edition): $300
  • ASME B31.3 (Piping Code): $350
  • API 579 (FFS): $300
  • Prep course (highly recommended): $2,500-$4,500
  • Total: $3,450-$5,450

Supplementary:

  • Practice exam question bank: $300-$500
  • ASNT UT reference materials: $100-$150
  • Piping materials reference: $100

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q1: Is API 570 harder than API 510 or 653?

A: Similar difficulty. All three exams: 200 questions, 4 hours, 75% pass score. First-time pass rate: 68-75% for all three. Most candidates find their weakest area determines success (for you it might be piping systems or RBI concepts).

Q2: How long should I study for API 570?

A: Budget 120-180 hours total preparation. If you have extensive piping experience (10+ years), 100 hours may suffice. If transitioning from vessel or other work, allocate 180+ hours. Use 6-8 week timeline for intensive study.

Q3: Can I take API 570 before API 510?

A: Yes. They're independent certifications. However, API 510 knowledge helps understand API 570 (both use RBI, API 579, similar inspection concepts). Many inspectors do 510 first due to broader knowledge base.

Q4: What if I don't have the full 3 years piping experience yet?

A: You must meet prerequisites to register. However, you can start studying now and plan exam for when you reach 3-year piping mark. In the meantime, focus on API 510 or 653 if you haven't gotten those.

Q5: Is the API 570 exam open-book?

A: No. You cannot bring reference materials into exam room. However, you CAN bring a basic calculator. Some testing centers allow you to have API 570 summary sheet, but verify with your testing center before exam day.

Q6: What's the job outlook after API 570 certification?

A: Excellent. Strong demand for API 570-certified inspectors in oil refining, petrochemicals, power generation. Salary: $80K-$120K for certified inspectors. Multi-certified (API 510/570/653): $120K-$180K. Consulting: $200-$400/hour. Job security: Very high (piping integrity essential to industry safety).

Q7: How often must I recertify?

A: API 570 certification valid 5 years. To recertify: Either retake full exam or demonstrate continued employment in NDT field + 40+ hours professional development. Maintaining is cheaper/easier than retesting.

Q8: Can I use API 570 to sign inspection reports?

A: Yes. API 570-certified inspectors are "inspection authority" and can sign off on in-service piping inspections. This signature authority is what makes API 570 valuable — you become the final decision-maker on acceptability.

Q9: What's the difference between API 570 and ASME B31.8 for piping inspection?

A: B31.8 is the design standard for gas transmission pipelines (buried); API 570 is for in-service inspection of aboveground piping in refineries/plants. Different scope, different certification requirements. You might need both if you work in pipeline operations.

Q10: Should I take API 510 before API 570?

A: Recommended but not required. API 510 knowledge helps contextualize vessel inspection concepts that overlap with piping (RBI, API 579, defect evaluation). However, if you have deep piping experience, you can start with API 570. Most inspectors eventually get both.

Conclusion

The API 570 certification requires serious preparation covering piping systems, inspection procedures, RBI strategy, defect evaluation, and repair procedures. With 120-180 hours of focused study, a quality prep course, and realistic practice exams, first-time pass rates exceed 80%. API 570 certification opens doors to lucrative inspection and consulting careers in global oil and gas industries.

Next Steps: Verify you meet prerequisites (ASNT Level III + 5 years NDT + 3 years piping), enroll in prep course, and plan 6-week intensive study timeline. Explore API 510 as complementary credential for multi-certified expertise.
